newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda, denying hand in Zaire war, to join summit.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda, denying hand in Zaire war, to join summit.

text.p: Rwanda said on Sunday it would attend a regional summit seeking to end fighting in Zaire but denied its troops had crossed the border to help Tutsi rebels.
A senior official said President Pasteur Bizimungu would go to the meeting in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on Tuesday.

Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, invited to the talks to represent his ailing president, Mobutu Sese Seko, accuses Rwandan troops of fighting alongside rebels inside Zaire and says that while they continue there can be no peace talks.

The presidents of six other regional states -- Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Cameroon, Uganda and Zambia -- are expected to attend the summit to tackle one of the region's most serious crises, which could lead to the breakup of Zaire.
"Our president has already confirmed attendance," Bizimungu's political adviser Seth Kamanzi told Reuters in the capital Kigali.

The Tuesday summit is the only prominent diplomatic initiative on the table to try to stop the fighting since last month and ease the plight of more than a million refugees whom foreign aid workers have had to abandon.
Government officials said that at the top of the agenda would be Zaire's accusations that Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army was fighting alongside the local Zairean Tutsi rebels.

The rebels have seized a string of towns along Zaire's eastern border with Burundi and Rwanda and are mopping up resistance in the city of Goma, headquarters of the world's biggest relief operation until aid workers fled on Saturday.

Among a million Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire in 1994 after Rwandan Tutsis took power are tens of thousands of armed Hutu militiamen blamed for the 1994 genocide of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Officials from the Organisation of African Unity said the Nairobi talks would seek to broker a ceasefire between Zaire's retreating army and the rebels, who seemed to have formed a broad alliance with other groups opposed to Mobutu's rule.

Reuters journalists saw Rwandan soldiers cross into Goma on Saturday, but Rwanda has persistently denied any presence in Zaire. However, the president and Vice-President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame say they morally support their cause.
Rwandan Army Chief of Staff Sam Kaka told Reuters on Sunday his battle-hardened troops never deployed inside Zaire, but only returned fire when attacked across the border by Zairean troops.
"There are no Rwandan troops in eastern Zaire, we never went there and we have no intention whatsoever of getting involved in that conflict," Kaka said.
He said those who were calling on Rwanda to withdraw its troops from Zaire were acting on false intelligence.
Kaka admitted Rwanda had shelled or fired on the Zairean towns of Bukavu and Goma in the past week but said this was in reply to Zairean aggression on Rwandan soil.
"We only responded after Zaire fired on our territory first. This was not an invasion but merely an action to neutralise hostile positions in Zaire," he said.

Pouring scorn on threats by his Zairean counterpart to hit back at Rwanda, he said his army was ready should they try: "They've failed to contain the rebels, how could they possibly deal with my army? We have a lot of experience of war and I see no problems at all in dealing with the Zairean army."
Zaire's Army Chief of General Staff, General Eluki Monga Aundu, on Saturday accused Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who is part Tutsi, of not doing enough to help soldiers at the front.
"We regret that the government is moving too slowly and has not yet given us the necessary means," he said, promising a counterattack inside Rwanda once the army had the equipment.
